blockers.title: TC-ACCEPT.maximal does not populate every designed field, and the resulting corpus-wide coverage hole is not named in notAuthored
blockers.detail: TC-ACCEPT.maximal.manifest.json (5f8df8215bc69e887f02a0b7fbaf3174f6af6dbbac237de8260f62fd214a7e15) leaves four designed field groups unpopulated: 'capabilities' is [], 'permissions' is [], 'configuration' is absent entirely, and no CommandSpec carries 'args'. I grepped the whole fixture directory: across all 51 authored and 13 supporting files there is ZERO occurrence of a 'configuration' object, zero 'capabilityId' (so every capabilities array in the corpus is empty), zero '"permission"' member (so every permissions array is empty), and zero 'args'. The maximal fixture is the only member of any class whose job is designed-field coverage, so these four groups have no exercise anywhere in the corpus.
blockers.whyItMatters: This is the attack-list case 'a required class member is missing or only named, not authored' in its subtler form: the member is authored under the right filename but does not meet the definition that makes it that member. Consequentially, two RJ-6 subcodes the schema defines - SELF_CLASSIFIED_CONFIGURATION and UNKNOWN_PERMISSION_TOKEN - are unreachable by every fixture in this corpus, and the host-owned classification-vocabulary validation that SRC-03 exists to enforce ('a component cannot ... classify its own hidden semantic input') has no positive fixture to validate against.
blockers.silenceAggravator: The corpus's notAuthored block names only three omissions (Windows-only TC-PATH, ENVELOPE_MISMATCH, DR-112 ceremony). None of these four is named there or anywhere else in the subject. The corpus therefore reads as complete on the TC-ACCEPT class while four designed field groups are silently uncovered - the pattern the dispatch names as 'silently claimed complete without naming the deferral'.
blockers.remedy: Either populate maximal with a capabilities entry, a permissions entry, a configuration block with host-vocabulary classifications, and a CommandSpec args array; or, if any of those is deliberately deferred to an owning row, name it in notAuthored with its deferral warrant the way D-002 is named for Windows.

blockers.title: Three required TC-NAME class members are unauthored and unnamed
blockers.requirementQuoted: /testCorpusRequirements/classes[TC-NAME]/requires: 'reserved root-command claim (name and alias forms)'; 'alias collision and alias-shadows-live'; 'parent-linkage collision and unknown/cyclic parent'
detail: ALIAS FORM OF THE RESERVED CLAIM: TC-NAME.reserved-root.manifest.json claims reserved root 'help' via manifest.name and its root command name. No fixture anywhere claims a reserved root command through an ALIAS. The complete alias inventory of the corpus is: alias-cycle {cmd-a, cmd-b}, alias-collision {fixture-min}, maximal {fx-max, fm}, and the stale-alias indexes {old-name}. None intersects reservedRootCommands ['help','version','doctor']. RJ-2's subcode ALIAS_SHADOWS_LIVE_OR_RESERVED has no fixture exercising its _OR_RESERVED arm.

ALIAS_COLLISION AS DISTINCT FROM ALIAS-SHADOWS-LIVE: the class lists both. TC-NAME.alias-collision.manifest.json declares aliases ['fixture-min'] where fixture-min is a live NAME - that is the alias-shadows-live member, and the fixture is named for the other one. No fixture presents an alias colliding with a live entry's ALIAS. RJ-2's ALIAS_COLLISION subcode is unexercised.

PARENT_LINKAGE_COLLISION: the class lists 'parent-linkage collision' separately from 'unknown/cyclic parent'. TC-NAME.unknown-parent and TC-NAME.parent-cycle cover the two arms of PARENT_UNKNOWN_OR_CYCLIC. The manifestSchema commands.commandSpecFields[parent] note defines the collision arm as a 'duplicate (parent,name) pair'. No fixture in the corpus carries a duplicate (parent,name) pair, and none carries a self-parent. RJ-2's PARENT_LINKAGE_COLLISION subcode has no fixture at all.
blockers.whyItMatters: TC-NAME is the class whose warrant is 'the full D-012 clause 7 negative-test enumeration, every member present and the walk checkable member by member'. Three members are not present, so the member-by-member walk the warrant promises cannot be completed against this corpus.
blockers.silenceAggravator: notAuthored names none of the three.
blockers.remedy: Author a manifest whose aliases include a reservedRootCommands member; a manifest whose alias equals a live entry's namesSnapshot alias; and a manifest with two commands sharing the same (parent, name) pair. Or name each in notAuthored with its warrant.

blockers.title: TC-NAME.stale-alias-after-window encodes a premature alias retirement that D-012 clause 5 forbids, and asserts non-resolution at a date on which the 90-day clock is still running
blockers.requirementQuoted: /testCorpusRequirements/classes[TC-NAME]/requires: 'inside the window (either clock unexpired) the alias MUST still resolve, and premature removal is itself a violation of D-012 clause 5's floor; after retirement past windowEndsNoEarlierThan (both clocks elapsed) the alias MUST NOT resolve'. manifestSchema/fields[aliases]/semantics: 'a rename keeps the old name as a deprecated alias for at least one host-core minor release cycle AND no fewer than 90 days from the deprecating release, whichever is longer'.
detail: DATE CLOCK STILL RUNNING. TC-NAME.index-stale-alias-after-window.json (f023c634161a2fd0e16f20791614bce5fda5d0ad3580b9cde0e8d1deed570bae) sets deprecatedAtDate 2026-06-01 and windowEndsNoEarlierThan 2026-07-01. 2026-06-01 + 90 days is 2026-08-30. The declared window end is 30 days after deprecation, i.e. 60 days SHORT of the mandatory floor - the index datum is itself unlawful under clause 5. The packet's asOf is 2026-08-14, which is day 74 of 90: the date clock is UNEXPIRED. Under the class's own rule ('either clock unexpired -> the alias MUST still resolve') the correct outcome at that asOf is RESOLVE. The fixture asserts 'TYPED non-resolve'.

RELEASE CLOCK HAS NO DATUM. 'Both clocks elapsed' requires evaluating the host-core minor release cycle. The index carries deprecatedAtRelease '0.1.0'; neither TC-NAME.stale-alias-after-window.packet.json (a2b4e4daf7ede4601ae1ed7ec19252728bd6dda684a4f7f95a8c84a6e27d646d, fields: kind, indexPath, alias, asOf, expected) nor the index carries a CURRENT host-core version. The lock fixtures carry hostCoreVersion '0.0.0-fixture'; the alias-resolution packets carry no equivalent. The release clock is therefore not evaluable from the fixture at all, so 'both clocks elapsed' is undecidable and the second clock is unexercised in both directions.
blockers.whyItMatters: This is not a labelling slip. As acceptance evidence, the fixture asserts that an implementation is CORRECT to stop resolving a deprecated alias 30 days after deprecation. That certifies precisely the premature removal the class text calls 'itself a violation of D-012 clause 5's floor'. An engine built to pass this corpus would be built to break clause 5. It is the one fixture in the corpus that, if satisfied, produces a wrong system.
blockers.remedy: Move windowEndsNoEarlierThan to a date at or after both clocks - e.g. deprecatedAtDate 2026-01-01 with windowEndsNoEarlierThan 2026-04-01 and asOf 2026-08-14 - and add a current host-core release datum to the packet so the release clock is evaluable. The inside-window sibling is correctly authored (deprecatedAtDate 2026-06-01, windowEndsNoEarlierThan 2026-12-01, asOf 2026-08-14: date clock unexpired, RESOLVE decidable) and should be the template.
blockers.notALabelDispute: I checked whether 'after window' could mean 'after windowEndsNoEarlierThan' alone, taking the declared date as authoritative. It cannot: the field is named windowEndsNoEarlierThan, i.e. a floor that the 90-day rule raises, not a value that overrides it. Reading the declared date as authoritative is what makes the fixture certify the violation.

blockers.title: The ACCEPT-side index fixtures silently adopt a resolution of open advisory V2-A1, and the scope-precedence index needs a key element beyond even that resolution
blockers.requirementQuoted: indexSchema/fields[entries]/entryShape/stableId: 'UUID - unique among LIVE entries per (stableId)'. component-manifest-schemas.v2.review-independent.json advisory V2-A1: 'entryShape.stableId's "unique among LIVE entries per (stableId)" phrasing sits in tension with the multi-version coexistence pair both records require ... a fixture author implementing the triggers literally would refuse TC-ACCEPT's own required fixture'.
detail: TC-ACCEPT.index-multiversion.json and TC-ACCEPT.index-all-accept.json each carry TWO entries with stableId 11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111, both status 'active' (both LIVE), at versions 0.0.1 and 0.0.2. Read literally against entryShape.stableId these indexes are invalid, and the second admission collides with the component's own first entry on name, mounted root command, and stableId uniqueness alike. The corpus asserts them ACCEPT. That is V2-A1's proposed repair - 'index entries are keyed per (stableId, version)' - applied as though it were the contract. V2-A1 is an ADVISORY on a CANDIDATE-NOT-APPLIED artifact; D-013 records it as 1 new advisory and no decision resolves it.

TC-NAME.index-scope-precedence.json goes further. Its two entries share stableId 1111..., the same provenance, AND the same version 0.0.1, differing only in scope ('global' with shadowedBy, and 'project'). That is a duplicate key under the literal rule AND under V2-A1's proposed (stableId, version) key. Admitting it requires a (stableId, version, scope) key that no governing source states - not the schema, not V2-A1, not D-012 clause 4 (which decides shadowing precedence and the disclosure obligation, not the entry key).
blockers.whyItMatters: Three of the corpus's ACCEPT and DISCLOSE outcomes are undecidable against the contract as written and are decidable only under an index entry-key rule the corpus never states. The subject's honestyRepairsThisRevision shows the author was working this exact seam - 'maximal and approved-exception now have distinct stableIds so they can coexist with minimal' is a workaround for V2-A1 - yet V2-A1 is not named anywhere in the subject, and the one place the tension cannot be dodged (the required multi-version coexistence pair) is authored as if it were settled.
blockers.remedy: Name V2-A1 in the subject and state which reading the corpus assumes, as a declared assumption pending the advisory's disposition; and either state the (stableId, version, scope) key the scope-precedence fixture needs, or rebuild that fixture on two distinct versions so it needs only V2-A1's proposed key.

shouldFix.title: TC-SIG.digest-mismatch's flipped byte lands inside manifest.name, so the fixture trips two refusal families with no precedence rule to choose between them
shouldFix.detail: I verified the flip mechanics exactly as claimed: TC-SIG.digest-mismatch.manifest.json differs from TC-ACCEPT.minimal.manifest.json in exactly one byte, at offset 120, 0x66 'f' -> 0x67 'g', same length 2100, and the packet's recorded manifestDigest 6f8203ff... is the UNFLIPPED source's digest. Honesty repair 2 is true as stated. But offset 120 sits inside the value of 'name': the flipped manifest reads name 'gixture-min' while its parent-less command is still named 'fixture-min'. Under manifestSchema/commands/rootNameBinding that is independently RJ-2/ROOT_COMMAND_NAME_MISMATCH. rejectionRules defines no evaluation order among RJ-1..RJ-6, so which family an admission emits is not decidable from the schema, while the corpus discipline requires 'exactly one refusal family/subcode'.
shouldFix.remedy: One byte. Flip inside a value with no structural role - e.g. the 'mounted root' description string - so RJ-4/DIGEST_MISMATCH is the only trigger. Re-pin the fixture digest and the corpus index entry.

shouldFix.title: Three RJ-2 fixtures are bare manifests with no packet supplying the index their expected outcome depends on, and two of them reuse ACCEPT-fixture stableIds
shouldFix.detail: TC-NAME.live-name-collision (stableId 2222...), TC-NAME.alias-collision (3333...) and TC-NAME.hostile-double-mount (4444...) all assert RJ-2 for collisions against LIVE names. A live name exists only in an index. Each is authored as a manifest alone with no packet naming an indexPath, so the expected outcome is not decidable from the subject's own bytes. The corpus already has the right pattern - all five TC-DUP fixtures are packets pairing manifestPath with indexPath, and they are correctly authored. Compounding it: 2222... is TC-ACCEPT.maximal's stableId and 4444... is TC-ACCEPT.approved-exception's. Paired with TC-ACCEPT.index-all-accept (the only index carrying both), live-name-collision presents stableId 2222 at version 0.0.1 against a live entry that is already stableId 2222 at version 0.0.1, so the refusal family becomes contested between RJ-1 and RJ-2. The schema also calls the hostile double-mount a 'pair'; it is authored as a single manifest.
shouldFix.remedy: Add three admission-against-index packets on the TC-DUP model, and give the two colliding manifests stableIds not used by any ACCEPT fixture (alias-collision's 3333... is already clean and is the model).

shouldFix.title: TC-SIG.lock-artifact-digest-mismatch contains no real bytes to mismatch against
shouldFix.detail: The class member is 'artifact bytes vs lock digest mismatch'. TC-SIG.lock-artifact-digest-mismatch.json records indexDigest 1111...1111, manifestDigest 2222...2222, artifactDigests[bin/entry] 3333...3333, and installId aaaaaaaa-... which matches no index in the corpus (every real index uses bbbbbbbb-...). Nothing in the fixture references stored bytes, so nothing recomputes and nothing can be compared: the mismatch is unfalsifiable rather than demonstrated. This is the one TC-SIG member not built on real bytes - its sibling TC-SIG.digest-mismatch is exact-byte and correct - and it sits against a corpus whose stated discipline is exact-byte authoring.
shouldFix.remedy: Rebuild it from TC-ACCEPT.lock-minimal-closure.json (which correctly pins indexDigest 723fe984... and real artifact digests) with exactly one artifactDigests entry altered, so the mismatch is against bytes that exist.

shouldFix.title: Eight of thirteen TC-PATH fixtures also violate the entrypoint-in-tree rule, so the class cannot discriminate between the path-rule arms
shouldFix.detail: In TC-PATH.absolute, .backslash, .dot, .dotdot, .drive-letter, .empty-segment, .non-nfc and .nul, the violating path REPLACES bin/entry in the committed tree while platforms[].entrypoint stays 'bin/entry'. Each therefore also trips RJ-3's 'entrypoint not present in the committed tree' clause - the same arm TC-PATH.entrypoint-absent exists to test. Because RJ-3 has no subcodes the stated expected outcome 'RJ-3' remains literally correct and singular, which is why this is SHOULD-FIX and not a blocker. But as acceptance evidence the class no longer discriminates: an implementation that checks only entrypoint presence and implements none of the '..', '.', absolute, backslash, drive-letter, empty-segment, non-NFC or NUL rules passes eight of thirteen. The four duplicate-path fixtures and symlink-escape correctly retain bin/entry and are unaffected.
shouldFix.remedy: Keep bin/entry in the tree in all eight and ADD the violating entry alongside it, as the duplicate-path fixtures already do.

advisories.title: index-multiversion's v0.0.2 entry carries the v0.0.1 signatureRef
advisories.detail: In TC-ACCEPT.index-multiversion.json the 0.0.2 entry has manifestDigest 3ae6676d3a7fda1eb9c57f8a69c4fb6a3b8bfa778dc3b2a4cff6cbdf174ebb09 but signatureRef 'sig:6f8203ff7b15b316' - the 0.0.1 digest prefix. Every other entry in the corpus follows 'sig:' + the first 16 hex of its own manifestDigest, and TC-ACCEPT.index-all-accept.json gives the same release the correct 'sig:3ae6676d3a7fda1e'. The two indexes disagree about the same admission. Envelope verification is DR-112's, so nothing here is decided by it; it is an internal inconsistency in pinned bytes.

advisories.title: TC-SIG.unsigned.packet.json omits 'expected'
advisories.detail: Every other packet in the corpus carries an 'expected' member. This one carries kind, manifestPath, manifestDigest, signatureEnvelope null and policyRequiresSignature true, and states no outcome. The corpus index supplies RJ-4/UNSIGNED, so the outcome is recorded somewhere; the fixture bytes alone do not state it, against the corpus's own discipline sentence 'Every authored fixture states expected outcome'.

advisories.title: TC-NAME-1 authors only the passing arm of the parity check, and records a rule rather than an outcome
advisories.detail: TC-NAME.reserved-list-live-grammar-parity.packet.json carries indexReservedRootCommands and liveHostGrammarReserved as equal lists, and states expected 'ACCEPT iff lists are equal'. The data does decide it - the lists are equal, so the outcome is ACCEPT - which is why this is advisory rather than a finding on decidability. But a CI parity check whose only fixture has the lists already equal cannot detect a parity checker that never compares. The divergent arm is unauthored and unnamed.

advisories.title: The no-execution probe's 'executable' cannot record execution
advisories.detail: TC-METADATA-ONLY.no-execution.packet.json declares containsExecutable dummy.onebyte with recordsExecution true. dummy.onebyte is one byte (2d711642b726b04401627ca9fbac32f5c8530fb1903cc4db02258717921a4881) and is the same file the ACCEPT manifests commit as bin/entry; it cannot record anything. The probe is declarative only. That is consistent with the corpus's own 'Does not execute fixtures' and with execution being DR-120's, so it is honest rather than wrong - but expectedRecorderExecutions 0 is currently satisfied by the absence of a recorder, not by the absence of execution.

advisories.title: The NFC / NFD / NUL classes carry their distinguishing codepoints as JSON escapes, not as raw bytes
advisories.detail: TC-PATH.non-nfc uses \u0301, TC-PATH.unicode-norm-duplicate pairs \u00e9 against e\u0301, and TC-PATH.nul uses \u0000. I verified the semantics are exactly right - non-nfc is genuinely NFD, the duplicate pair is byte-distinct and NFC-equal, and no file contains a raw NUL - so these fixtures are correct and decidable. The note is only that the class byteRule's stated rationale ('indistinguishable at the rendered-text level and exist only as pinned bytes') is not literally met: the escapes are plainly visible in the rendered text. The escape form is defensible; the rationale sentence and the fixtures no longer describe each other.

advisories.title: Command-level aliases are not carried into namesSnapshot, and nothing exercises whether they should be
advisories.detail: TC-ACCEPT.maximal declares a component alias 'fx-max' and a command alias 'fm'. TC-ACCEPT.index-all-accept records namesSnapshot.aliases ['fx-max'] only. That is defensible - commandSpecFields[aliases] scopes sub-command aliases 'to the mounted subtree' - but namesSnapshot exists so 'RJ-2's collision universe contains it by construction, not by inference', and whether command aliases enter that universe is left to inference. No fixture tests a collision against a command-level alias.
